Definition: of Hebrew origin (H531); Amos, an Israelite:--Amos.
BiblicalUsage: The name Amos belongs to three different men, and the Bible keeps them apart by their stories: the prophet Amos was a herdsman from Tekoa whom God sent to Israel with a word of judgment two years before the earthquake, and who told Amaziah plainly that he was no prophet and no prophet's son, only a herdsman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit. In Matthew's genealogy the same Greek name stands for King Amon, son of Manasseh and father of Josiah — the English Bibles spell him Amon — and in Luke's genealogy there is another Amos altogether, the son of Naum and father of Mattathias, an otherwise unknown link in the line of Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: What I take from the name is that God uses ordinary men — a herdsman with no credentials — and also keeps His promise through kings who failed and ancestors nobody remembers. The prophet's words outlived the kingdoms he spoke against, and the genealogies remind me that every link in the chain mattered, whether the man was famous or forgotten.
